messages.author: c0eb6fbaa553325e
messages.subject: Repeated phenotype
parts:
Hi all,

I want to perform a QTL analysis of a phenotype, analyzed twice in different places and different times. In such data, not all individuals overlap between both experiments, and some of which that overlap have shown different results between these two experiments. Single QTL analysis shows several QTLs, but neither of them mapped in the same locus. I wonder if there are way to combine the data to analyze this phenotype at the same time in order to increase the confidence.
Thanks in advance

messages.author: 2502c952822e4f47
messages.subject: Re: Repeated phenotype
parts:
Hello,

I think you could either do a meta-analysis or use the program MAPQTL, which can combine data for a single phenotype if you have an integrated map from the two sets of data.

For both of these strategies the individuals you would consider should be different. That is, the two sets should not include any common individual(s). The individuals should have been generated independently by different crosses.

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Repeated phenotype
parts:
Because you have measured the same (but not all) individuals in the two environments/times, I think you should be fitting a mixed effects model, to account for the within-individual correlation. However, unfortunately, R/qtl doesn't have any functions for this.

karl

messages.author: a34fd766eb53b108
messages.subject: Re: Repeated phenotype
parts: Have you analysing your data using, e.g. REML, to partition into variance components?  You could add occasion to your experimental design and get weighted line means to use as input for the qtl analysis.  Also check to see the normality of your data before you analyses it (it may need to be transformed).  if the individuals differ greatly in phenotype score across environments then this may hint that the trait has a strong environmental component - and low heritability.  Therefor if you do three mapping exercises, 1. exp1; 2. exp2; 3 across exps and illustrate all qtls on the same linkage map you can look at which qtl differ between occasions and which if any are robust across occasions.  i agree with the previous comments.
